qs.q: Which diagnostic blood parameter finding is characteristic of hereditary haemochromatosis due to iron overload?
qs.e: Haemochromatosis is characterized by high ferritin and transferrin saturation greater than 60%. Positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies are instead found in primary biliary cholangitis.

ai.title: Hereditary Haemochromatosis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A genetic iron overload disorder presenting with liver, cardiac and endocrine damage. Diagnosis relies on iron studies, genetic testing and imaging when available. Management centres on phlebotomy and monitoring.

sections.p: Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused mainly by HFE C282Y homozygosity, leading to increased intestinal iron absorption and systemic deposition.
b: Iron studies: serum ferritin >300 ng/mL (men) or >200 ng/mL (women), transferrin saturation >45%

t.b: Elevated ferritin indicates iron overload; high levels may be due to inflammation, so interpret with transferrin saturation
High saturation (>45%) confirms excess iron absorption; normalises after treatment
Positive C282Y homozygosity confirms diagnosis; heterozygotes are at lower risk

sections.p: Staging follows the Liver Staging System: Stage 0 (no fibrosis) to Stage 4 (cirrhosis). Cardiac and endocrine involvement are graded separately.

t.b: Non‑invasive assessment of liver stiffness; values >12 kPa suggest cirrhosis

sections.p: The classic cause is HFE mutation. In low‑resource settings, secondary causes such as chronic haemolysis, repeated transfusions, hepatitis B/C and alcohol must be excluded.
b: Secondary iron overload: transfusion, chronic liver disease, malaria, HIV

t.b: Differentiates primary from secondary: very high ferritin (>1000) suggests secondary
Rule out viral hepatitis as a cause of liver injury

sections.p: Patients often appear well but may have fatigue, arthralgia, diabetes, liver dysfunction and skin pigmentation. Cardiac symptoms appear late.
b: Heart failure signs in advanced disease

t.b: Mildly raised ALT/AST; pattern is hepatocellular

sections.p: Work‑up focuses on iron indices, liver assessment and cardiac evaluation. In resource‑poor settings, basic tests guide management.

t.b: High ferritin suggests overload; normalise after phlebotomy
Detects hepatomegaly or cirrhosis; if unavailable, clinical signs of portal hypertension are used

sections.p: Early recognition prevents irreversible organ damage. Watch for signs of cirrhosis, heart failure and hypogonadism.
First line is therapeutic phlebotomy. Adjuncts include dietary iron restriction and monitoring for complications. Avoid iron chelators unless phlebotomy is contraindicated.
b: Therapeutic phlebotomy every 2–4 weeks until ferritin <50 ng/mL

t.b: Reduces iron stores; chosen for safety and cost
Limit red meat and fortified foods; advise vitamin C avoidance with iron

sections.p: Regular monitoring of ferritin and transferrin saturation is essential. Family members should be screened.

t.b: Ensures iron stores remain low; rising levels indicate relapse

sections.p: Other causes of liver disease and iron overload can mimic haemochromatosis.

t.b: Both NAFLD and hepatitis raise ALT/AST; ferritin and saturation help differentiate

sections.p: Inflammation or infection can raise ferritin, masking true iron status. Transferrin saturation can be low in anaemia of chronic disease.

t.b: Elevated in inflammation; interpret with transferrin saturation

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of acute liver failure, severe heart failure, or sudden drop in haemoglobin

faq.q: Can diet alone control iron overload?
faq.a: No, diet reduces intake but does not remove excess iron; phlebotomy is required.
Not mandatory but confirms diagnosis and guides family screening.

faq.q: What if a patient cannot tolerate phlebotomy?
faq.a: Consider iron chelation therapy, though it is less preferred due to cost and side effects.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with fatigue and elevated ferritin presents. What is the first investigation? — Serum transferrin saturation to confirm iron overload.
A patient with known haemochromatosis develops new diabetes. What is the likely mechanism? — Pancreatic iron deposition causing beta‑cell dysfunction.
During phlebotomy, the patient develops hypotension. What should you do? — Stop the procedure, give IV fluids and monitor vitals.
A patient with high ferritin but normal transferrin saturation is found to have chronic hepatitis B. What is the next step? — Treat the hepatitis and reassess iron studies after viral control.
A 60‑year‑old woman with skin bronzing has normal liver enzymes. What complication should you screen for? — Cardiac involvement; obtain ECG and echocardiogram.
A patient refuses phlebotomy. What alternative therapy is acceptable? — Oral iron chelation with deferasirox, noting its cost and monitoring needs.
